arXiv:2006.08628v2 [astro-ph.CO] 02 Mar 2021

Peeling off foregrounds with the constrained moment ILC method to unveil primordial CMB BB-modes

Mathieu Remazeilles ††thanks: E-mail:˜mathieu.remazeilles@manchester.ac.uk    Aditya Rotti ††thanks: E-mail:˜aditya.rotti@manchester.ac.uk    Jens Chluba ††thanks: E-mail:˜jens.chluba@manchester.ac.uk Affiliation: Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics, School of Physics and Astronomy, The University of Manchester, Oxford Road, Manchester, M13 9PL, U.K.
Accepted –. Received
Abstract

Galactic foregrounds are the main obstacle to observations of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) BB-mode polarization. In addition to obscuring the inflationary BB-mode signal by several orders of magnitude, Galactic foregrounds have non-trivial spectral signatures that are partially unknown and distorted by averaging effects along the line-of-sight, within the pixel/beam window, and by various analysis choices (e.g., spherical harmonic transforms and filters). Statistical moment expansion methods provide a powerful tool for modeling the effective Galactic foreground emission resulting from these averaging effects in CMB observations, while blind component separation treatments can handle unknown foregrounds. In this work, we combine these two approaches to develop a new semi-blind component separation method at the intersection of parametric and blind methods, called constrained moment ILC (cMILC). This method adds several constraints to the standard ILC method to de-project the main statistical moments of the Galactic foreground emission. Applications to maps are performed in needlet space and when compared to the NILC method, this helps significantly reducing residual foreground contamination (bias, variance, and skewness) in the reconstructed CMB BB-mode map, power spectrum, and tensor-to-scalar ratio. We consider sky-simulations for experimental settings similar to those of LiteBIRD and PICO, illustrating which trade-offs between residual foreground biases and degradation of the constraint on rr can be expected within the new cMILC framework. We also outline several directions that require more work in preparation for the coming analysis challenges.

Keywords: 
cosmic microwave background – inflation – early universe – polarization – methods: analytical – observational

1 Introduction

The search for the primordial BB-mode polarization (curl-like pattern) of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation is recognised as one of the ultimate challenges in CMB cosmology. The primordial CMB BB-mode signal would indeed be a clear signature of the primordial gravitational waves of quantum origin predicted by inflation (Starobinsky, 1983, e.g.), when the Universe underwent ultra-rapid accelerated expansion just about 10−35{10^{-35}} seconds after the Big Bang. The amplitude of the primordial CMB BB-mode power spectrum, parametrised using the tensor-to-scalar ratio rr, would allow determining the energy scale of inflation: V1/4≃(r/0.01)1/4×1016{V^{1/4}\simeq(r/0.01)^{1/4}\times 10^{16}} GeV (Knox & Song, 2002), and there by distinguish main classes of early Universe models (Baumann et al., 2009; Martin et al., 2014, e.g.,).

One of the main goals for next-generation CMB experiments is a statistically significant detection of primordial CMB BB-modes down to r≃10−3r\simeq 10^{-3}. From space, this effort is led by LiteBIRD (Hazumi et al., 2019), whose launch is planned by JAXA for early 2028. Another space concept is PICO (Hanany et al., 2019), which is currently in NASA’s concept study phase. In addition, ambitious future missions with a broad range of capabilities including CMB spectroscopy are being discussed for the ESA Vogage 2050 program (Delabrouille et al., 2019; Basu et al., 2019; Chluba et al., 2019). From the ground, the Simons Observatory (Ade et al., 2019, SO;), whose survey should start in 2021, and the CMB-S4 (Abazajian et al., 2016) project are relentlessly moving forward. For all these efforts, CMB foregrounds pose a real challenge because the BB-mode signal is extremely faint (≤50\leq 50  nK r.m.s fluctuations), with intense polarized Galactic emission (mostly synchrotron and thermal dust emission) obscuring it by several orders of magnitude. In addition, gravitational lensing effects on the CMB by the large-scale structure and several inst rumental systematics create spurious contamination to CMB BB-modes. Component separation methods are thus critical, since the residual foreground contamination in the recovered CMB BB-mode map will set the ultimate uncertainty limit with which rr can be determined (Remazeilles et al., 2018).

Several component separation methods have been developed in the literature to disentangle the primary CMB signal from the foregrounds: Commander (Eriksen et al., 2008), SMICA (Delabrouille et al., 2003; Cardoso et al., 2008), NILC (Delabrouille et al., 2009), SEVEM (Fernández-Cobos et al., 2012), and GNILC (Remazeilles et al., 2011b), to name only those that have been used for the data product release of the ESA’s Planck satellite (Planck Collaboration et al., 2018b). These methods (which have been successfully applied to Planck temperature and EE-mode data for which the signal-to-foregrounds ratio was relatively large) are now being recycled, along with most recent algorithms like xForecast (Stompor et al., 2016; Errard et al., 2016), BFoRe (Alonso et al., 2017) and tailored template fitting (Ichiki et al., 2019, Delta-map;), for new faint signal-to-foregrounds regimes in BB-mode forecasts (Remazeilles et al., 2018, e.g.,).

Some of these methods, like the Bayesian fitting method Commander and maximum-likelihood fitting method xForecast, are parametric since they rely on astrophysical models of the foreground emission, while other methods, like the variance-minimization method NILC, are blind in the sense that no explicit assumption is made on foregrounds. Each of them have their advantages and weaknesses, but consistency between blind and parametric methods on CMB BB-mode reconstruction is desired for claiming a robust detection. In this respect, many lessons have been learned (Flauger et al., 2014; BICEP2/Keck Collaboration et al., 2015), and we now understand the importance of further developing component separation methods for BB-modes that allow us to eliminate biases arising from residual foregrounds. In addition, the optimal method depends on the observable that is targeted, and there may be no one-rules-it-all approach.

Component separation methods rely on the distinct spectral signatures of the various components of emission (CMB, foregrounds) to disentangle them in multi-frequency sky observations. However, Galactic foregrounds have non-trivial spectral energy distributions (SEDs), whose exact properties are still unknown at the sensitivity levels of r≃10−3r\simeq 10^{-3}. In parametric approaches, a slight mismodelling of the foregrounds may lead to large biases on rr due to huge amplitude disparity between foregrounds and primordial BB-modes (Remazeilles et al., 2016; Hensley & Bull, 2018). Similarly, the thermal dust emission from the interstellar medium is expected to be partially decorrelated across frequencies, i.e. the dust spectral parameters (spectral index and temperature) may not only vary across the sky but also across frequencies, because of the averaging of multiple cloud contributions of different spectral indices and temperatures along the line-of-sight (Tassis & Pavlidou, 2015). Thus, while still sufficient at Planck sensitivity, the common modelling of the dust SED as a unique modified blackbody across frequencies may break at the targeted BB-mode sensitivity, and lead to significant biases on rr after component separation.

To minimize the effects of unknown foreground complexities, blind analysis methods provide a powerful remedy, while averaging effects of known SEDs can in principle be modeled parametrically through moment expansion methods (Stolyarov et al., 2005; Chluba et al., 2017). Aside from line-of-sight averaging effects, similar spectral averaging effects arise from the limited beam/pixel resolution of the sky maps and various analysis choices, such as spherical harmonic decomposition, downgrading the resolution, or generally when applying filters (Chluba et al., 2017). The effective SED of the foreground emission in a given pixel/beam may therefore differ from the expected SED shape in each line-of-sight, since the former is the average over several line-of-sight SEDs.

As an illustration (see Fig. 1), let us assume that, in each single pixel of a high-resolution sky map, the synchrotron emission can be accurately described by a single power-law, fsync​(ν)≃νβf_{\rm sync}(\nu)\simeq\nu^{\thinspace\beta}, across frequencies ν\nu, with a pixel-dependent spectral index β⁡(p)\beta(p) varying across the sky. While this SED model might be approximately valid at the given map resolution and sensitivity, it can actually break for maps of lower angular resolution, for which the effective SED is now the average of multiple power-laws within a larger beam:

⟨fsync​(ν)⟩=⟨νβ⁡(p)⟩\displaystyle\langle f_{\rm sync}(\nu)\rangle=\langle\nu^{\thinspace\beta(p)}\rangle (1)
≃⟨e⟨β⟩​ln⁡ν+(β−⟨β⟩)​deβ​ln⁡νd​β|β=⟨β⟩+12​(β−⟨β⟩)2​d2​eβ​ln⁡νd​β2|β=⟨β⟩⟩\displaystyle\simeq\left<{\rm e}^{\langle\beta\rangle\ln\nu}+\left(\beta-\langle\beta\rangle\right){{\rm d}{\rm e}^{\beta\ln\nu}\over{\rm d}\beta}|_{\beta=\langle\beta\rangle}+{1\over 2}\left(\beta-\langle\beta\rangle\right)^{2}{{\rm d}^{2}{\rm e}^{\beta\ln\nu}\over{\rm d}\beta^{2}}|_{\beta=\langle\beta\rangle}\right> (2)
≃e⟨β⟩​ln⁡ν​⟨1+(β−⟨β⟩)​ln⁡ν+12​(β−⟨β⟩)2​(ln⁡ν)2⟩\displaystyle\simeq{\rm e}^{\langle\beta\rangle\ln\nu}\left<1+\left(\beta-\langle\beta\rangle\right)\ln\nu+{1\over 2}\left(\beta-\langle\beta\rangle\right)^{2}\left(\ln\nu\right)^{2}\right> (3)
≃e⟨β⟩​ln⁡ν​(1+12​⟨β2−⟨β⟩2⟩​(ln⁡ν)2)≃ν⟨β⟩+C​ln⁡ν.\displaystyle\simeq{\rm e}^{\langle\beta\rangle\ln\nu}\left(1+{1\over 2}\langle\beta^{2}-\langle\beta\rangle^{2}\rangle\left(\ln\nu\right)^{2}\right)\simeq\nu^{\thinspace\langle\beta\rangle+C\ln\nu}. (4)

Here, we defined the beam-average ⟨Y⁡(p,ν)⟩≡⟨Y⁡(p,ν)⟩p∈beam⁡[ν]\langle Y(p,\nu)\rangle\equiv\langle Y(p,\nu)\rangle_{p\thinspace\in\thinspace{\rm beam}[\nu]}. As Eq. (4) shows, the average SED is no longer a power-law but a curved power-law at lower angular resolution, with an effective curvature C=12​⟨β​(p)2−⟨β⟩2⟩{C={1\over 2}\langle\beta(p)^{2}-\langle\beta\rangle^{2}\rangle} given by the variance (second-order moment) of the spectral index within the beam (Chluba et al., 2017). In the last step, we resummed the series, which assumes that all higher order moment are Gaussian, which in general may not be valid. Therefore, while the spectral intensity of the synchrotron might be accurately modelled by a power-law at one resolution, the power-law model is no longer valid at lower angular resolution. This results in an effective decorrelation of the foreground emission across frequencies. For similar reasons, omitting effective curvature due to beam averaging in the SED modelling of thermal dust can induce non-negligible biases on r≲10−3r\lesssim 10^{-3} (Remazeilles et al., 2018). Modelling as many moments of the foreground emission as possible, given the sensitivity limits of an experiment, thus provides a natural way for capturing some of the additional complexity of the CMB foreground contamination.

With this in mind, in this work we develop a semi-blind component separation method, called constrained moment ILC (cMILC), which operates at the intersection of blind ILC methods and parametric foreground modelling methods. We extend the NILC method by adding several nulling constraints on the effective SEDs of the main moments of the dust and synchrotron emissions in order to remove the bulk of the residual foreground contamination in the recovered CMB BB-mode map. This is achieved by combining the moment expansion technique (Chluba et al., 2017) with the Constrained ILC method (Remazeilles et al., 2011a). While here the focus is on BB-mode signal, this type of semi-blind approach has broader applicability and was recently introduced for the extraction of the relativistic Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) effect (Remazeilles & Chluba, 2020) and CMB spectral distortions (Rotti & Chluba, 2021). In harmonic space, the power of moment methods was furthermore recently explored on Planck data (Mangilli et al., 2019). Moment expansion techniques have also been used in the modeling of SZ signals (Chluba et al., 2013). First-order moments have also been recently used to augment internal template fitting methods for BB-mode foreground cleaning (Ichiki et al., 2019).

The paper is organised as follows. In Sect. 2, we review the basics of the ILC and Constrained ILC methods. In Sect. 3, we present our new semi-blind component separation method cMILC, which plugs the foreground moment expansion technique described in Sect. 3.1 into the Constrained ILC method, as outlined in Sect. 3.2. We discuss the statistical properties of residual foregrounds and noise in Sect. 3.4. We then present the results of our BB-mode analysis on sky simulations for experimental settings similar to LiteBIRD and PICO in Sect. 4. We discuss some directions for optimisation of the method in Sect 5, and draw our conclusions in Sect. 6.

2 Basics of ILC methods

2.1 The standard ILC

The standard internal linear combination (Bennett et al., 2003; Tegmark et al., 2003; Eriksen et al., 2004; Delabrouille et al., 2009; Basak & Delabrouille, 2012, ILC;) is a blind component separation method as there is no attempt at directly modelling the foregrounds. Hence, the sky observations dν​(p)d_{\nu}(p), at each frequency ν\nu and for each pixel pp are written as

dν​(p)=aν​s​(p)+nν​(p),\displaystyle d_{\nu}(p)=a_{\nu}\thinspace s(p)+n_{\nu}(p), (5)

where aνa_{\nu} is the known spectral response (SED)11 1 Modelled by the first temperature derivative of the blackbody spectrum. of the CMB anisotropies s⁡(p)s(p) at frequency ν\nu, while nν​(p)n_{\nu}(p) is the un-modelled overall contamination from foregrounds and instrumental noise.

For convenience with the algebra, we recast Eq. (5) in a nf×1n_{f}\times 1 vector form, where nfn_{f} is the number of frequency channels:

𝒅⁡(p)=𝒂​s​(p)+𝒏⁡(p).\displaystyle\boldsymbol{d}(p)=\boldsymbol{a}s(p)+\boldsymbol{n}(p). (6)

Here, 𝒅⁡(p)={dν​(p)}ν\boldsymbol{d}(p)=\{d_{\nu}(p)\}_{\nu} collects the set of available frequency maps, 𝒂={aν}ν\boldsymbol{a}=\{a_{\nu}\}_{\nu} is the known CMB SED vector, s⁡(p)s(p) corresponds to the unknown CMB anisotropies that we aim at extracting, and 𝒏⁡(p)={nν​(p)}ν{\boldsymbol{n}(p)=\{n_{\nu}(p)\}_{\nu}} collects the un-modelled foregrounds and noise that we aim at mitigating in the reconstructed CMB map.

The standard ILC estimate, s^​(p)\hat{s}(p), of the CMB anisotropies is obtained by forming a weighted linear combination of the frequency maps

s^=∑νwν​dν≡𝒘T​𝒅\displaystyle\hat{s}=\sum_{\nu}w_{\nu}\thinspace d_{\nu}\equiv\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{d} (7)

that is of minimum variance, i.e.

∂∂𝒘​⟨s^ 2⟩=0.\displaystyle{\partial\over\partial\boldsymbol{w}}\langle\hat{s}^{\thinspace 2}\rangle=0. (8)

Here, the ILC weights 𝒘={wν}ν\boldsymbol{w}=\{w_{\nu}\}_{\nu} assigned to the frequency maps are constrained to provide unit response to the CMB SED:

𝒘T​𝒂=1\displaystyle\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{a}=1 (9)

in order to guarantee the full conservation of the CMB signal s⁡(p)s(p) in the variance minimization. This ensures that the ILC estimate

s^=𝒘T​𝒅=𝒘T​(𝒂​s+𝒏)=s+𝒘T​𝒏\displaystyle\hat{s}=\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\left(\boldsymbol{a}s+\boldsymbol{n}\right)=s+\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{n} (10)

does not alter the CMB signal ss [i.e. no multiplicative error thanks to the constraint Eq. (9)], while the variance of the residual foreground and noise 𝒘T​𝒏\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{n} is minimized by Eq. (8).

The variance of the ILC map, ⟨s^ 2⟩\langle\hat{s}^{\thinspace 2}\rangle, relates to the covariance of the data 𝒅\boldsymbol{d} as

⟨s^ 2⟩=𝒘T​⟨𝒅​𝒅T⟩​𝒘=𝒘T​𝐂​𝒘,\displaystyle\langle\hat{s}^{\thinspace 2}\rangle=\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\langle\boldsymbol{d}\boldsymbol{d}^{\rm T}\rangle\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}, (11)

where 𝐂=⟨𝒅​𝒅T⟩\boldsymbol{\rm C}=\langle\boldsymbol{d}\boldsymbol{d}^{\rm T}\rangle is the nf×nfn_{f}\times n_{f} covariance matrix of the data whose elements are Cν​ν′=⟨dν​dν′⟩{\rm C}_{\nu\nu^{\prime}}=\langle d_{\nu}d_{\nu^{\prime}}\rangle for any pair of frequencies (ν,ν′)\left(\nu,\nu^{\prime}\right). An empirical estimate of the data covariance matrix in each pixel pp can be obtained by ergodicity:

𝐂⁡(p)=1Np​∑p′∈𝒟⁡(p)𝒅⁡(p′)​𝒅​(p′)T,\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rm C}(p)={1\over N_{p}}\sum_{p^{\prime}\in\thinspace\mathcal{D}(p)}\boldsymbol{d}(p^{\prime})\boldsymbol{d}(p^{\prime})^{\rm T}, (12)

where 𝒟⁡(p)\mathcal{D}(p) is a domain of pixels surrounding pixel pp, and NpN_{p} the number of pixels in this domain.

The ILC weights 𝒘\boldsymbol{w} are thus the solution of the constrained variance-minimization problem:

{∂∂𝒘​(𝒘T​𝐂​𝒘)=0,𝒘T​𝒂=1,\begin{cases}{\partial\over\partial\boldsymbol{w}}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}\right)=0,\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{a}=1,\end{cases} (13)

which can be addressed with a Lagrange multiplier λ\lambda by solving

∂∂𝒘​[𝒘T​𝐂​𝒘+λ⁡(1−𝒘T​𝒂)]=0.\displaystyle{\partial\over\partial\boldsymbol{w}}\left[\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}+\lambda\left(1-\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{a}\right)\right]=0. (14)

This yields 𝒘T=λ​𝒂T​𝐂−1{\boldsymbol{w}^{T}=\lambda\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}}, while 𝒘T​𝒂=1\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{a}=1 leads to λ=(𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝒂)−1{\lambda=\left(\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\thinspace\boldsymbol{a}\right)^{-1}}, so that the standard ILC weights are given by

𝒘T=(𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝒂)−1​𝒂T​𝐂−1.\displaystyle\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}=\left(\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\thinspace\boldsymbol{a}\right)^{-1}\thinspace\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}. (15)

2.2 The Constrained ILC (cILC)

While the variance of the global contamination (i.e. foregrounds plus noise) is minimized by the standard ILC estimate, this is not necessarily the solution with minimal foreground variance. Instead of minimizing the variance of the global contamination, the Constrained ILC (cILC) method (Remazeilles et al., 2011a) extends the standard ILC to fully eliminate selected foreground residuals by using prior knowledge on their SED and adding orthogonality constraints to the variance-minimization problem:

{∂∂𝒘​(𝒘T​𝐂​𝒘)=0𝒘T​𝒂=1𝒘T​𝒃1=0𝒘T​𝒃m=0,\begin{cases}{\partial\over\partial\boldsymbol{w}}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}\right)=0\\ \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{a}=1\\ \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{1}=0\\ \vdots\\ \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{m}=0,\end{cases} (16)

where 𝒃1,⋯,𝒃m\boldsymbol{b}_{1},\cdots,\boldsymbol{b}_{m} are the SED vectors of mm modelled foreground components, to which the cILC weights 𝒘\boldsymbol{w} are orthogonal. If we write the sky observations as

𝒅⁡(p)=𝒂​s​(p)+∑i=1m𝒃i​gi​(p)+𝒏⁡(p),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{d}(p)=\boldsymbol{a}\thinspace s(p)\thinspace+\thinspace\sum_{i=1}^{m}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\thinspace g_{i}(p)\thinspace+\boldsymbol{n}(p), (17)

where {gi​(p)}1≤i≤m\{g_{i}(p)\}_{1\leq i\leq m} are the mm foreground components whose SEDs {𝒃i}1≤i≤m\{\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq m} are modelled, while 𝒏⁡(p)\boldsymbol{n}(p) includes un-modelled foregrounds and instrumental noise, then the orthogonality constraints 𝒘T​𝒃i=0\boldsymbol{w}^{T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}=0 of the cILC method in Eq. (16) guarantee the full cancellation of the residual foreground contamination from the mm modelled components in the reconstructed CMB map:

s^​(p)\displaystyle\hat{s}(p) =(𝒘T​𝒂)​s​(p)+∑i=1m(𝒘T​𝒃i)​gi​(p)+𝒘T​𝒏​(p)\displaystyle=\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{a}\right)\thinspace s(p)\thinspace+\thinspace\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\right)\thinspace g_{i}(p)\thinspace+\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{n}(p) (18)
=s⁡(p)+𝒘T​𝒏​(p).\displaystyle=s(p)+\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{n}(p). (19)

This significantly differs from the ILC method (Eq. 13) which suffers from additional foreground residuals as ∑i=1m(𝒘T​𝒃i)​gi​(p)≠0\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\right)\thinspace g_{i}(p)\neq 0 in this case. However, the penalty of adding nulling constraints on some foregrounds in the cILC is an increase of the noise residuals 𝒘T​𝒏​(p)\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{n}(p) compared to the standard ILC. But there is a sweet spot between noise cost and reduction of foreground biases, as we show in this work. This optimization furthermore depends on the observable that is targeted, which in our case is rr (see Sect. 4.2).

If we introduce the nf×(m+1)n_{f}\times(m+1) SED matrix 𝐀=[𝒂𝒃1⋯𝒃m]{\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}=[\boldsymbol{a}\thinspace\boldsymbol{b}_{1}\thinspace\cdots\boldsymbol{b}_{m}]}, whose columns collect the SED vectors of the modelled components, and the 1×(m+1)1\times(m+1) transposed vector 𝒆T=[1 0⋯ 0]{\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}=[1\thinspace 0\thinspace\cdots\thinspace 0]}, then the system of equations (16) can be rewritten in the compact form:

{∂∂𝒘​(𝒘T​𝐂​𝒘)=0𝒘T​𝐀=𝒆T.\begin{cases}{\partial\over\partial\boldsymbol{w}}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}=\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}.\end{cases} (20)

Hence, the problem is equivalent to solving

∂∂𝒘​[𝒘T​𝐂​𝒘+ΛT​(𝒆−𝐀T​𝒘)]=0,\displaystyle{\partial\over\partial\boldsymbol{w}}\left[\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}+\Lambda^{\rm T}\left(\boldsymbol{e}-\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{w}\right)\right]=0, (21)

where ΛT=[λμ1⋯μm]\Lambda^{\rm T}=[\lambda\thinspace\mu_{1}\thinspace\cdots\thinspace\mu_{m}] is a vector of (m+1)(m+1) Lagrange multipliers. This yields to 𝒘T=ΛT​𝐀T​𝐂−1{\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}=\Lambda^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}}, while the constraints 𝒘T​𝐀=𝒆T{\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}=\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}} give ΛT=𝒆T​(𝐀T​𝐂−1​𝐀)−1{\Lambda^{\rm T}=\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}\left(\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}\right)^{-1}}. The cILC weights are then given by

𝒘T=𝒆T​(𝐀T​𝐂−1​𝐀)−1​𝐀T​𝐂−1,\displaystyle\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}=\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}\left(\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}, (22)

which is a generalization of Eq. (15). Equation  (22) has been previously derived in the literature for the extraction of the relativistic SZ effect (Remazeilles & Chluba, 2020) and CMB spectral distortions (Rotti & Chluba, 2021). Similar multidimensional ILC filters have been derived for other component separation methods like GNILC (Remazeilles et al., 2011b) and MILCA (Hurier et al., 2013), the main difference between them lying in the form of the mixing matrix 𝐀\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}.

It should be noted that for a single orthogonality constraint, i.e. 𝐀=[𝒂​𝒃]{\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}=[\boldsymbol{a}\thinspace\boldsymbol{b}]} and 𝒆T=[1 0]{\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}=[1\thinspace 0]}, the general expression Eq. (22) reduces to

𝒘T=(𝒃T​𝐂−1​𝒃)​𝒂T​𝐂−1−(𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝒃)​𝒃T​𝐂−1(𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝒂)​(𝒃T​𝐂−1​𝒃)−(𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝒃)2,\displaystyle\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}={\left(\boldsymbol{b}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\right)\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}-\left(\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\right)\boldsymbol{b}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\over\left(\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{a}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{b}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\right)-\left(\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\right)^{2}}, (23)

which was introduced by Remazeilles et al. (2011a) to null SZ cluster residuals in primary CMB maps, when 𝒂\boldsymbol{a} and 𝒃\boldsymbol{b} are the SEDs of CMB and thermal SZ, respectively. Finally, in the absence of any orthogonality constraint, i.e. 𝐀≡𝒂\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}\equiv\boldsymbol{a} and 𝒆≡1\boldsymbol{e}\equiv 1, the expression Eq. (22) reduces to the standard ILC given in Eq. (15).

3 Semi-blind component separation method

We now work out our new semi-blind component separation method for BB-modes, the constrained moment ILC (cMILC), which combines foreground moment expansion (Chluba et al., 2017) and cILC method (Remazeilles et al., 2011a).

3.1 Moment expansion of the foreground emission

The spectral intensity22 2 By ”intensity”, we mean either II, QQ, UU, EE, or BB, without loss of generality. of the Galactic foreground emission depends on several spectral parameters 𝜷⁡(p)≡{βi​(p)}1≤i≤n\boldsymbol{\beta}(p)\equiv\{\beta_{i}(p)\}_{1\leq i\leq n} (e.g. spectral indices, temperatures) that vary across the sky (hence the pp dependence for ’pixel’) and along the line-of-sight:

I⁡(ν,p)=Aν0​(p)​f​(ν,𝜷⁡(p)).\displaystyle I(\nu,p)=A_{\nu_{0}}(p)\thinspace f\left(\nu,\boldsymbol{\beta}(p)\right). (24)

Aν0​(p)A_{\nu_{0}}(p) is the amplitude of the foreground emission at some pivot frequency ν0\nu_{0}, and f⁡(ν,𝜷⁡(p))f\left(\nu,\boldsymbol{\beta}(p)\right) is the spectral energy distribution (SED) which varies both across frequencies ν\nu and across the sky, depending on the local spectral parameters 𝜷⁡(p)≡{βi​(p)}1≤i≤n\boldsymbol{\beta}(p)\equiv\{\beta_{i}(p)\}_{1\leq i\leq n}.

As stressed by Chluba et al. (2017), we can expand the foreground SED, f⁡(ν,𝜷⁡(p))f\left(\nu,\boldsymbol{\beta}(p)\right), in terms of statistical moments around some fixed pivot parameters 𝜷¯≡{β¯i}i\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\equiv\{\overline{\beta}_{i}\}_{i}:

f⁡(ν,𝜷⁡(p))\displaystyle f\left(\nu,\boldsymbol{\beta}(p)\right) (25)
=\displaystyle= ∑k∑α1+⋯+αn=k(β1(p)−β¯1)α1⋯(βn(p)−β¯n)αnα1!⋯αn!∂kf⁡(ν,𝜷¯)∂β¯1α1⋯∂β¯nαn⋅\displaystyle\sum_{k}\sum_{\alpha_{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{n}=k}{\left(\beta_{1}(p)-\overline{\beta}_{1}\right)^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\left(\beta_{n}(p)-\overline{\beta}_{n}\right)^{\alpha_{n}}\over\alpha_{1}!\cdots\alpha_{n}!}{\partial^{\thinspace k}f\left(\nu,\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right)\over\partial\overline{\beta}_{1}^{\thinspace\alpha_{1}}\cdots\partial\overline{\beta}_{n}^{\thinspace\alpha_{n}}}\cdot (26)

This is nothing but a multi-dimensional Taylor series in all the spectral parameters, however, it gives the flexibility to describe various physical and observational averaging processes. The moment expansion highlights that the foreground emission can be captured by a set of moment components in the sky:

mα1,⋯,αn​(p)=Aν0​(p)​(β1(p)−β¯1)α1⋯(βn(p)−β¯n)αnα1!⋯αn!,\displaystyle m_{\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{n}}(p)=A_{\nu_{0}}(p)\thinspace{\left(\beta_{1}(p)-\overline{\beta}_{1}\right)^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\left(\beta_{n}(p)-\overline{\beta}_{n}\right)^{\alpha_{n}}\over\alpha_{1}!\cdots\alpha_{n}!}, (27)

each of them having a uniform SED across the sky given by

∂α1+⋯+αnf∂β1α1⋯∂βnαn​(ν,𝜷⁡(p)=𝜷¯).\displaystyle{\partial^{\thinspace\alpha_{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{n}}f\over\partial\beta_{1}^{\thinspace\alpha_{1}}\cdots\partial\beta_{n}^{\thinspace\alpha_{n}}}\left(\nu,\boldsymbol{\beta}(p)=\overline{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right). (28)

Below, we will consider thermal dust and synchrotron as the main polarized Galactic foregrounds for BB-modes. The SED of the synchrotron emission is known to be close to a power-law

fsync​(ν,βs​(p))=(ννs)βs​(p),\displaystyle f_{\rm sync}\left(\nu,\beta_{s}(p)\right)=\left({\nu\over\nu_{s}}\right)^{\beta_{s}(p)}, (29)

for data in Rayleigh-Jeans brightness temperature units, with an average spectral index of ⟨βs​(p)⟩p≃−3\langle\beta_{s}(p)\rangle_{p}\simeq-3 over the sky (Kogut et al., 2007; Miville-Deschênes et al., 2008; Krachmalnicoff et al., 2018; Planck Collaboration et al., 2018b). Conversely, the SED of the thermal dust emission is known to be close to a modified blackbody

fdust​(ν,βd​(p),Td​(p))=(ννd)βd​(p)+1​1exp⁡(h​νk​Td​(p))−1,\displaystyle f_{\rm dust}\left(\nu,\beta_{d}(p),T_{d}(p)\right)=\left({\nu\over\nu_{d}}\right)^{\beta_{d}(p)+1}{1\over\exp\left({h\nu\over kT_{d}(p)}\right)-1}, (30)

for data in Rayleigh-Jeans brightness temperature units, with an average spectral index of ⟨βd​(p)⟩p≃1.5\langle\beta_{d}(p)\rangle_{p}\simeq 1.5 and an average temperature of ⟨Td​(p)⟩p≃20\langle T_{d}(p)\rangle_{p}\simeq 20 K (Planck Collaboration XI, 2014; Planck Collaboration X, 2016; Planck Collaboration Int. XLVIII, 2016).
