By choosing pivot parameters that are close to the expected mean of the spectral parameters over the sky, β¯s=⟨βs​(p)⟩p≃−3{\overline{\beta}_{s}=\langle\beta_{s}(p)\rangle_{p}\simeq-3}, β¯d=⟨βd​(p)⟩p≃1.5{\overline{\beta}_{d}=\langle\beta_{d}(p)\rangle_{p}\simeq 1.5}, and T¯d=⟨Td​(p)⟩p≃20{\overline{T}_{\!d}=\langle T_{d}(p)\rangle_{p}\simeq 20} K, we ensure that the bulk of the Galactic foreground emission projects onto the zeroth-, first-, and second-order moments. However, a detailed optimization is more complicated as we briefly discuss in Sect. 5.1.

3.2 The constrained moment ILC (cMILC)

Our semi-blind component separation method cMILC aims at recovering the CMB BB-mode polarization signal from sky observations by adding nulling constraints on the main foreground moments in the cILC framework in order to improve the removal of the Galactic foreground contamination compared to standard ILC methods, which rely only on simple variance minimization. We thus build the cMILC method by enforcing the following constraints:

{∂∂𝒘​(𝒘T​𝐂​𝒘)=0𝒘T⋅𝒂=1𝒘T⋅𝒇s​y​n​c​(β¯s)=0𝒘T⋅∂β¯s𝒇s​y​n​c​(β¯s)=0𝒘T⋅∂β¯s2𝒇s​y​n​c​(β¯s)=0𝒘T⋅𝒇d​u​s​t​(β¯d,T¯d)=0𝒘T⋅∂β¯d𝒇d​u​s​t​(β¯d,T¯d)=0𝒘T⋅∂T¯d𝒇d​u​s​t​(β¯d,T¯d)=0𝒘T⋅∂β¯d2𝒇d​u​s​t​(β¯d,T¯d)=0𝒘T⋅∂T¯d2𝒇d​u​s​t​(β¯d,T¯d)=0𝒘T⋅∂β¯d∂T¯d𝒇d​u​s​t​(β¯d,T¯d)=0.\begin{cases}{\partial\over\partial\boldsymbol{w}}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\boldsymbol{a}=1\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\boldsymbol{f}_{sync}\left(\overline{\beta}_{s}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial_{\overline{\beta}_{s}}\boldsymbol{f}_{sync}\left(\overline{\beta}_{s}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial^{2}_{\overline{\beta}_{s}}\boldsymbol{f}_{sync}\left(\overline{\beta}_{s}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}\left(\overline{\beta}_{d},\overline{T}_{\!d}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial_{\overline{\beta}_{d}}\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}\left(\overline{\beta}_{d},\overline{T}_{\!d}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial_{\overline{T}_{d}}\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}\left(\overline{\beta}_{d},\overline{T}_{\!d}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial^{2}_{\overline{\beta}_{d}}\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}\left(\overline{\beta}_{d},\overline{T}_{\!d}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial^{2}_{\overline{T}_{d}}\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}\left(\overline{\beta}_{d},\overline{T}_{\!d}\right)=0\\[4.2679pt] \boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial_{\overline{\beta}_{d}}\partial_{\overline{T}_{d}}\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}\left(\overline{\beta}_{d},\overline{T}_{\!d}\right)=0.\end{cases} (42)

It is important to stress that cMILC does not attempt to fit the foregrounds, which are spatially correlated and uncertain components, but instead aims at deprojecting the dominant foreground moments in sky maps without altering the CMB component. Thus, bulk of the Galactic foreground contamination that is spatially correlated with the deprojected moments is eliminated from the recovered CMB BB-mode power spectrum. Any remaining unconstrained foreground contribution is just variance-minimised, like in blind methods.44 4 Hence, the exact pivots parameters do not need to be absolutely known (Fig. 11), although pivots can help optimizing the method (see Sect. 5.1).

The cMILC weights are thus again given by Eq. (22):

𝒘cMILCT=𝒆T​(𝐀T​𝐂−1​𝐀)−1​𝐀T​𝐂−1,\displaystyle\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}_{\rm cMILC}=\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}\left(\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}, (43)

where, when limiting constraints to zeroth- and first-order moments as an example, the SED matrix 𝐀\boldsymbol{{\rm A}} is a nf×6n_{f}\times 6 matrix given by

𝐀=(𝒂𝒇s​y​n​c𝒇d​u​s​t∂β¯s𝒇s​y​n​c∂β¯d𝒇d​u​s​t∂T¯d𝒇d​u​s​t),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}=\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{a}&\boldsymbol{f}_{sync}&\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}&\partial_{\overline{\beta}_{s}}\boldsymbol{f}_{sync}&\partial_{\overline{\beta}_{d}}\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}&\partial_{\overline{T}_{d}}\boldsymbol{f}_{dust}\end{pmatrix}, (44)

and the vector 𝒆\boldsymbol{e} is given by

𝒆T=(100000).\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}. (45)

The SED matrix 𝐀\boldsymbol{{\rm A}} and vector 𝒆\boldsymbol{e} can be augmented by including higher-order moments, depending on the sensitivity floor of the experiment. We stress that by applying the Woodbury formula to Eq. (53), the cILC/cMILC filter Eq. (43) reduces to 𝒆T​(𝐀T​𝐍−1​𝐀)−1​𝐀T​𝐍−1\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}(\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}})^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}^{-1}, where, unlike maximum-likelihood parametric fitting methods (Stompor et al., 2016, e.g.), the covariance matrix 𝐍\boldsymbol{{\rm N}} here does not only account for the noise but also for the unconstrained foregrounds (e.g. unmodelled foregrounds or higher-order moments) that may be omitted in the mixing matrix 𝐀\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}. The data covariance matrix 𝐂\boldsymbol{\rm C} in Eq. (43) thus allows for blind variance minimization of any remaining unparameterized foregrounds but also of possible residuals that would arise from suboptimal pivot choices (see Fig. 11 in Appendix A).

For our analysis, we will be applying several cMILC filters (see Table 1) to the sky simulations by considering more and more columns in the SED matrix 𝐀\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}, starting from the standard ILC method without nulling constraints (i.e. 𝐀≡𝒂\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}\equiv\boldsymbol{a}), and ending with the fully-constrained moment ILC with all the nulling constraints on zeroth-, first-, and second-order foreground moments (i.e. with a nf×10n_{f}\times 10 SED matrix 𝐀\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}). This progressive approach will help to highlight how increasing the number of moment constraints affects the trade-offs between foreground and noise residuals (bias, variance, and higher-order statistics) in the recovered CMB BB-mode map, power spectrum, and tensor-to-scalar ratio. Below we will see that the optimal number of moments is a function of the experimental sensitivity and spectral coverage.

3.3 Needlet implementation

ILC filtering can be implemented directly in pixel space on the sky maps dν​(p)d_{\nu}(p) (Bennett et al., 2003; Eriksen et al., 2004, e.g.) or in harmonic space on spherical harmonic coefficients aν​(ℓ,m)a_{\nu}(\ell,m) of the sky maps (Tegmark et al., 2003, e.g.). Since pixel-space ILC methods are fully local in pixel space, they are nonlocal in harmonic space because of uncertainty principle, hence all multipoles are given the same weights. Similarly, harmonic-space ILC methods being fully local in multipole space are nonlocal in pixel space and thus provide same weights to all pixels of a sky map. Nonlocal weights in either pixel or multipole space are not optimal for component separation, since the local conditions of contamination by foregrounds and noise vary both across the sky and across multipoles.

Because of their localisation properties both in pixel space and harmonic space, spherical wavelets such as needlets (Narcowich et al., 2006; Guilloux et al., 2009) provide a powerful alternative to allow the ILC weights to adjust themselves depending on local conditions of contamination both across the sky and across angular scales (Delabrouille et al., 2009). Therefore, in this work we implement both ILC and cMILC methods on the same needlet frame, so that hereafter the standard ILC method will be referred to as NILC for needlet ILC (Delabrouille et al., 2009), while our needlet-based constrained moment ILC method is still referred to as cMILC.

Needlet decomposition is performed on BB-mode sky maps at each frequency as follows. We first define a set of seven bandpass windows {h(j)​(ℓ)}1≤j≤7\{h^{(j)}(\ell)\}_{1\leq j\leq 7} of cosine shape in harmonic space (Fig. 3), following the prescription of Basak & Delabrouille (2013). Each needlet window isolates a subrange of multipoles or angular scales, while the whole set satisfies the property ∑j=17(h(j)​(ℓ))2=1{\sum_{j=1}^{7}(h^{(j)}(\ell))^{2}=1} in order to not lose any power in the data processing. The number and width of needlet windows were chosen to allow decent localization in harmonic space while conserving sufficient localization in pixel space for efficient foreground cleaning, by following a dyadic scheme with wider windows at high multipoles to ensure more localization in pixel space for the cleaning of small-scale fluctuations in sky maps. The number, width and shape of the needlet windows are free parameters and different prescriptions have been used in the literature depending on the observable of interest (Planck Collaboration XXII, 2016, e.g.), thus leaving room for further optimisation (see Sect. 5). The spherical harmonic coefficients aν​(ℓ,m)a_{\nu}(\ell,m) of the frequency maps are then bandpass filtered by the needlet windows as a~ν(j)​(ℓ,m)=h(j)​(ℓ)​aν​(ℓ,m){\tilde{a}^{(j)}_{\nu}(\ell,m)=h^{(j)}(\ell)\thinspace a_{\nu}(\ell,m)}. The inverse spherical harmonic transform of the bandpass-filtered harmonic coefficients a~ν(j)​(ℓ,m)\tilde{a}^{(j)}_{\nu}(\ell,m) then yields seven needlet maps d~ν(j)​(p)\tilde{d}^{\thinspace(j)}_{\nu}(p) for each frequency. Each needlet map thus contains typical anisotropies of specific angular scales selected by the needlet window. The ILC weights at all frequencies are then computed for each needlet scale (j)(j) independently, so that we obtain seven ILC CMB maps s^(j)​(p)=∑νwν(j)​(p)​d~ν(j)​(p){\widehat{s}^{\thinspace(j)}(p)=\sum_{\nu}w_{\nu}^{(j)}(p)\tilde{d}^{\thinspace(j)}_{\nu}(p)} for each needlet frame. The spherical harmonic coefficients, s^(j)​(ℓ,m)\widehat{s}^{\thinspace(j)}(\ell,m), of the seven needlet ILC CMB maps are then bandpass-filtered again as z^(j)​(ℓ,m)=h(j)​(ℓ)​s^(j)​(ℓ,m){\widehat{z}^{\thinspace(j)}(\ell,m)=h^{(j)}(\ell)\thinspace\widehat{s}^{\thinspace(j)}(\ell,m)}, and inverse spherical-harmonic transformed into maps z^(j)​(p)\widehat{z}^{\thinspace(j)}(p), which are finally coadded to form the complete NILC or cMILC CMB map s^​(p)=∑j=17z^(j)​(p){\widehat{s}(p)=\sum_{j=1}^{7}\widehat{z}^{\thinspace(j)}(p)}.

3.4 Statistics

In this section, we first compare the statistics of the constrained ILC (cILC, cMILC) and standard ILC (NILC) approaches, by generalizing the formulas of the ILC variance (Tegmark et al., 2003; Delabrouille et al., 2009, e.g.) to our cMILC filter. We then illustrate our findings on simulations in Sect. 4.2.2. We stress that, while the standard ILC is the solution of minimum overall variance (foregrounds plus noise), cMILC leads to the solution of minimum foreground variance. In particular, cMILC beats the standard ILC in terms of residual foreground contamination (bias, variance, and skewness) thanks to nulling constraints, but at the cost of larger residual noise contamination due to the increased volume of the parameter space. However, there is an optimal trade-off point for cMILC, where the noise penalty is largely compensated by the significant reduction of the residual foreground bias. Aside from experimental parameters, this sweet spot depends on the observable and here we consider rr as figure of merit (see Figs. 8 and 9 in Sect. 4.2), illustrating the gains for both the variance and the bias on rr through the cumulative systematic and statistical error δ​r=(r−rtrue)2+σ2​(r)\delta r={\sqrt{(r-r^{\thinspace\rm true})^{2}+\sigma^{2}(r)}}.

3.4.1 Overall variance

Using Eq. (11) and Eq. (15), we recover the standard expression (Tegmark et al., 2003, e.g.) for the variance of the ILC map55 5 Note that in the derivation of the standard formulas Eqs. (46)-(47) for the variance we make the assumption that empirical correlations between the weights 𝒘⁡(p)\boldsymbol{w}(p) and the data d⁡(p)d(p) can be neglected to first order, and thus the weights can be pulled out of ⟨⋯⟩\langle\cdots\rangle in Eq. (11).:

σILC2\displaystyle\sigma_{\rm ILC}^{2} ≡⟨s^ILC2⟩=𝒘ILCT​𝐂​𝒘ILC=1𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝒂,\displaystyle\equiv\langle\hat{s}^{2}_{\rm ILC}\rangle=\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}={1\over\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{a}}, (46)

where 𝐂=⟨𝒅​𝒅T⟩\boldsymbol{\rm C}=\langle\boldsymbol{d}\boldsymbol{d}^{T}\rangle is the nf×nfn_{f}\times n_{f} covariance matrix of the data, and 𝒂\boldsymbol{a} is the SED for CMB. Similarly, by using Eq. (43) we can derive the expression for the variance of the cMILC map, σcMILC2≡⟨s^cMILC2⟩\sigma^{2}_{\rm cMILC}\equiv\langle\hat{s}^{2}_{\rm cMILC}\rangle:

σcMILC2\displaystyle\sigma_{\rm cMILC}^{2} =𝒘cMILCT​𝐂​𝒘cMILC=𝒆T​(𝐀T​𝐂−1​𝐀)−1​𝒆,\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}=\boldsymbol{e}^{T}(\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm A}})^{-1}\boldsymbol{e}, (47)

where 𝐀=[𝒂𝒃1⋯𝒃m]{\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}=[\boldsymbol{a}\thinspace\boldsymbol{b}_{1}\thinspace\cdots\boldsymbol{b}_{m}]} is the nf×(m+1)n_{f}\times(m+1) SED matrix for the CMB and the constrained foreground moments (e.g. Eq. 44), and 𝒆T=[1 0⋯ 0]{\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}=[1\thinspace 0\thinspace\cdots\thinspace 0]}.

By defining the submatrix 𝐁=[𝒃1⋯𝒃m]{\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}=[\boldsymbol{b}_{1}\thinspace\cdots\boldsymbol{b}_{m}]} as the nf×mn_{f}\times m SED matrix for the modelled foreground moments only, the full SED matrix 𝐀\boldsymbol{{\rm A}} can be written in the block matrix form:

𝐀=(𝒂𝐁),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\rm A}}=\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{a}&\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}\end{pmatrix}, (48)

so that the variance of the cMILC map Eq. (47) reads as

σcMILC2=𝒆T​(𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝒂𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝐁𝐁T​𝐂−1​𝒂𝐁T​𝐂−1​𝐁)−1​𝒆.\displaystyle\sigma_{\rm cMILC}^{2}=\boldsymbol{e}^{\rm T}\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{a}&\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}\\ \boldsymbol{{\rm B}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{a}&\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\boldsymbol{e}. (49)

Using block matrix inversion, the variance of the cMILC map reduces to

σcMILC2\displaystyle\sigma_{\rm cMILC}^{2} =σILC21−σILC2​𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝐁​(𝐁T​𝐂−1​𝐁)−1​𝐁T​𝐂−1​𝒂.\displaystyle={\sigma_{\rm ILC}^{2}\over 1\thinspace-\thinspace\sigma^{2}_{\rm ILC}\thinspace\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}\thinspace\left(\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{a}}. (50)

Therefore, the overall variance of the cMILC map is larger than the overall variance of the standard ILC map, with an amplification factor of

σcMILC2σILC2=11−σILC2​𝒂T​𝐂−1​𝐁​(𝐁T​𝐂−1​𝐁)−1​𝐁T​𝐂−1​𝒂≥1.\displaystyle{\sigma_{\rm cMILC}^{2}\over\sigma_{\rm ILC}^{2}}={1\over 1\thinspace-\thinspace\sigma^{2}_{\rm ILC}\thinspace\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}\thinspace\left(\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{{\rm B}}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{\rm C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{a}}\geq 1. (51)

This increase of the overall variance is expected, since the volume of the parameter space (number of modelled components) is larger for the cMILC than for the standard ILC. However, while the standard ILC is the solution of minimum overall variance, it is not the solution of minimum foreground variance. As we show below, cMILC yields lower foreground contamination than standard ILC.

3.4.2 Foregrounds residual variance

Let us model the data with independent contributions from the various components:

𝒅⁡(p)=𝒂​s​(p)+∑i=1m𝒃i​gi​(p)+𝒏⁡(p),\displaystyle\boldsymbol{d}(p)=\boldsymbol{a}\thinspace s(p)\thinspace+\thinspace\sum_{i=1}^{m}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\thinspace g_{i}(p)\thinspace+\boldsymbol{n}(p), (52)

where s⁡(p)s(p) is the CMB signal and 𝒂\boldsymbol{a} its SED, {gi​(p)}1≤i≤m\{g_{i}(p)\}_{1\leq i\leq m} the mm foreground components whose SEDs {𝒃i}1≤i≤m\{\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq m} are constrained in cMILC, while not in the ILC, and 𝒏⁡(p)\boldsymbol{n}(p) the contamination from both instrumental noise and un-modelled foregrounds. The covariance matrix of the data thus reads as

𝐂=𝒂​σs2​𝒂T+∑i=1m𝒃i​σgi2​𝒃iT+𝐍,\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rm C}=\boldsymbol{a}\thinspace\sigma_{s}^{2}\thinspace\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\thinspace+\thinspace\sum_{i=1}^{m}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\thinspace\sigma_{g_{i}}^{2}\thinspace\boldsymbol{b}_{i}^{\rm T}\thinspace+\thinspace\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}, (53)

where σs2=⟨s​(p)2⟩{\sigma_{s}^{2}=\langle s(p)^{2}\rangle} is the variance of intrinsic CMB anisotropies, σgi2=⟨gi​(p)2⟩{\sigma_{g_{i}}^{2}=\langle g_{i}(p)^{2}\rangle} the variance of the modelled foregrounds, and 𝐍=⟨𝒏⁡(p)​𝒏​(p)T⟩{\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}=\langle\boldsymbol{n}(p)\boldsymbol{n}(p)^{T}\rangle} the covariance matrix of the noise and un-modelled foregrounds.

By inserting Eq. (53) into Eq. (46), the contribution from the different components to the overall variance of the standard ILC map becomes explicit:

σILC2\displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{\rm ILC} =𝒘ILCT​(𝒂​σs2​𝒂T+∑i=1m𝒃i​σgi2​𝒃iT+𝐍)​𝒘ILC\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}^{\rm T}\left(\boldsymbol{a}\thinspace\sigma_{s}^{2}\thinspace\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\thinspace+\thinspace\sum_{i=1}^{m}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\thinspace\sigma_{g_{i}}^{2}\thinspace\boldsymbol{b}_{i}^{\rm T}\thinspace+\thinspace\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}\right)\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC} (54)
=σs2+∑i=1m(𝒘ILCT​𝒃i)2​σgi2+𝒘ILCT​𝐍​𝒘ILC,\displaystyle=\sigma_{s}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\right)^{2}\sigma_{g_{i}}^{2}+\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}, (55)

since 𝒘ILCT​𝒂=1\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{a}=1, but 𝒘ILCT​𝒃i≠0\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\neq 0. In contrast to the ILC solution, the variance of the cMILC map Eq. (47) reduces to:

σcMILC2\displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{\rm cMILC} =𝒘cMILCT​(𝒂​σs2​𝒂T+∑i=1m𝒃i​σgi2​𝒃iT+𝐍)​𝒘cMILC\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}^{\rm T}\left(\boldsymbol{a}\thinspace\sigma_{s}^{2}\thinspace\boldsymbol{a}^{\rm T}\thinspace+\thinspace\sum_{i=1}^{m}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\thinspace\sigma_{g_{i}}^{2}\thinspace\boldsymbol{b}_{i}^{\rm T}\thinspace+\thinspace\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}\right)\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC} (56)
=σs2+𝒘cMILCT​𝐍​𝒘cMILC,\displaystyle=\sigma_{s}^{2}+\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}, (57)

since 𝒘cMILCT​𝒂=1\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{a}=1 and 𝒘cMILCT​𝒃i=0\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}=0. Therefore, the variance of the cMILC map is cleared of any contribution from the constrained foregrounds (Eq. 56), while some residual variance from those foregrounds still contributes to the variance of the standard ILC map (Eq. 54). If we now consider that the unconstrained foreground moments are those which are below the noise of the instrument, then 𝒘ILCT​𝐍​𝒘ILC\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC} and 𝒘cMILCT​𝐍​𝒘cMILC\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC} are just the noise variance contributions to the standard ILC and cMILC maps, and hence cMILC moves towards the solution with minimum residual foreground contamination, unlike the standard ILC. Consequently, the inequality Eq. (51) on overall variance implies that the residual noise variance must be larger in the cMILC map than in the standard ILC map, i.e. 𝒘cMILCT​𝐍​𝒘cMILC≥𝒘ILCT​𝐍​𝒘ILC{\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}\geq\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{{\rm N}}\thinspace\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm ILC}}.

To conclude, cMILC reduces the variance and bias from residual foreground contamination, while it has larger noise variance than the standard ILC. By including more and more foreground moments in cMILC, the residual noise variance increases in the CMB map, but in contrast the residual foreground variance decreases towards the minimum foreground variance solution, thus largely beating the standard ILC. These theoretical expectations are confirmed by our analysis on sky simulations (see Fig. 6).

While foreground residuals and noise residuals both cause biases on the CMB BB-mode power spectrum, and hence on the inferred tensor-to-scalar ratio rr, the noise bias can be corrected for (i.e., by Jackknife), such that any bias on a detection arises from foreground residuals, not from instrumental noise residuals. In this respect, the cMILC method focuses on nulling foreground biases at the expense of increased noise variance.

3.4.3 Higher-order statistics

By realizing that CMB and instrumental noise are mostly Gaussian fields compared to Galactic foregrounds which are highly non-Gaussian, it becomes clear that cMILC will get rid of most non-Gaussian residuals in the CMB map through nulling constraints, while the standard ILC will not. As an illustration, the skewness of the reconstructed CMB map reads:

⟨s^3⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{s}^{3}\rangle =⟨s3⟩+∑i,j,k=1m(𝒘T​𝒃i)​(𝒘T​𝒃j)​(𝒘T​𝒃k)​⟨gi​gj​gk⟩+⟨(𝒘T​𝒏)3⟩\displaystyle=\langle s^{3}\rangle\thinspace+\thinspace\sum_{i,j,k=1}^{m}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{j}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{k}\right)\langle g_{i}\thinspace g_{j}\thinspace g_{k}\rangle\thinspace+\thinspace\langle\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{n}\right)^{3}\rangle
≃∑i,j,k=1m(𝒘T​𝒃i)​(𝒘T​𝒃j)​(𝒘T​𝒃k)​⟨gi​gj​gk⟩,\displaystyle\simeq\sum_{i,j,k=1}^{m}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{j}\right)\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{k}\right)\langle g_{i}\thinspace g_{j}\thinspace g_{k}\thinspace\rangle, (58)

where in the last line we assumed that CMB and noise are mostly Gaussian and have negligible skewness, i.e. ⟨s3⟩≃0{\langle s^{3}\rangle\simeq 0} and ⟨𝒏3⟩≃0{\langle\boldsymbol{n}^{3}\rangle\simeq 0}. By construction, the cMILC weights give 𝒘cMILCT​𝒃i=0\boldsymbol{w}_{\rm cMILC}^{\rm T}\boldsymbol{b}_{i}=0, such that the skewness due to foreground residuals in Eq. (58) should reduce to zero for the cMILC map, while this is not the case for the standard ILC map. These expectations are also confirmed by our analysis on sky simulations (see Fig. 6). While this work focuses on BB-modes, we refer to Sect. 5 for a brief discussion of the potential benefits of reducing non-Gaussian residuals for primordial non-Gaussianity and CMB lensing analyses.

4 Analysis

4.1 Sky simulations

In our sky simulations, we consider different models of the foreground emission, capitalizing on existing tools. For PICO, we use the public PICO sky simulations66 6 https://zzz.physics.umn.edu/ipsig/20180424_dc_maps (models 91 and 96)., which have been delivered on NERSC as an open data analysis challenge. These include both the PySM d1s1 model (Thorne et al., 2017), which is consistent with Planck observations, and a more complicated dust model derived from MHD simulations (Kritsuk et al., 2018) that has non-trivial spectral dependence and accounts for line-of-sight effects, as we discuss in Sect. 4.2.5. For LiteBIRD, since there is no available public simulation, we replicated the PySM d1s1 model of the public PICO simulation with specifications given in Table 2.

We first evaluate the performance of our semi-blind component separation method cMILC on the PySM sky simulations d1s1 for both LiteBIRD and PICO experiments, and compare the results of cMILC with those obtained with the standard NILC method. The simulated sky maps in polarization for the model d1s1 include several components of emission: CMB anisotropies with a tensor-to-scalar ratio of r=0r=0, an optical depth to reionization of τ=0.054\tau=0.054 and full lensing contamination (AL=1A_{\rm L}=1); Galactic thermal dust emission as a modified blackbody component with varying spectral index and temperature across the sky, based on the Planck Commander maps (Planck Collaboration X, 2016); and Galactic synchrotron emission as a power-law component with varying spectral index across the sky, based on the template maps from Miville-Deschênes et al. (2008). For more details regarding PySM and its implementation we refer to Thorne et al. (2017).

The sky emission is integrated over either LiteBIRD (Table 2) or PICO frequency bands (Table 3), for which current simulations assume δ\delta-function bandpasses. Each frequency map has a HEALPix Nside=512N_{\rm side}=512 pixelisation scheme (Górski et al., 2005), and is smoothed with a Gaussian beam of FWHM values listed in Tables 2-3. Gaussian white noise map realisations of typical r.m.s. values listed in the aforementioned tables were then co-added to the sky maps. Therefore, we have 15 sky maps ranging from 4040 GHz to 402402 GHz for the LiteBIRD-like simulation, and 21 sky maps ranging from 2020 GHz to 800800 GHz for the PICO simulation.

We perform foreground removal by applying the NILC and cMILC methods to these two sets of sky maps, and study the impact on CMB BB-mode reconstruction (map, power spectrum, and tensor-to-scalar ratio) of deprojecting more and more foreground moments with cMILC, with combinations as listed in Table 1. For our analysis, we first transform the Stokes Q,UQ,U full-sky maps into full-sky BB-mode maps at each frequency, then apply the NILC and cMILC methods on the set of full-sky BB-mode observations, thus avoiding EE-to-BB leakage inherent to masking procedures. To obtain numerically stable results, it was important to carefully consider the precision settings of the linear algebra routines. The CMB BB-mode map reconstruction is performed at 40′40^{\prime} angular resolution for both LiteBIRD and PICO. As a main figure of merit we use rr, but we expect other observables such as ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} and NeffN_{\rm eff} to also benefit from cMILC (see discussion in Sect. 5).

4.2 Results

4.2.1 Visual inspection of recovered maps in the BICEP2 region

While the reconstruction of the CMB BB-mode map from the LiteBIRD and PICO sky maps by the NILC and cMILC methods is performed on the entire sky, for illustration we first inspect the quality of the reconstructed maps and their residual foreground and noise contamination in the BICEP2 region (BICEP2 Collaboration et al., 2014). This allows us to better appreciate the improvement in foreground removal with cMILC in comparison to NILC. To evaluate residual foreground and noise contamination in the reconstructed CMB BB-mode map after component separation, we applied the same NILC/cMILC weights that were assigned in the reconstruction of the CMB BB-mode map to the input foreground and noise maps of the simulations.

Figure 4 summarizes the results for LiteBIRD in the BICEP2 region. The first row shows the NILC results, while the following rows show the cMILC results when including progressively more constraints on foreground moments, starting in the second row with cMILC03 which deprojects zeroth-order moments (fsync,fdust){(f_{\rm sync},f_{\rm dust})}, and ending in the bottom row with cMILC08 which deprojects both zeroth- and first-order moments (fsync,fdust,∂βsfsync,∂βdfdust,∂Tdfdust){(f_{\rm sync},f_{\rm dust},\partial_{\beta_{s}}f_{\rm sync},\partial_{\beta_{d}}f_{\rm dust},\partial_{T_{d}}f_{\rm dust})}. No further constraints on second-order moments were imposed in cMILC because the noise degradation prevented us from probing higher-order moments of the foreground emission.

The residual foreground contamination left by each method is shown in the first column: clearly, the level of residual foregrounds is significantly reduced in the cMILC CMB BB-mode maps when including more and more moments in the component separation. The second and third columns show respectively the residual noise fluctuations and the recovered CMB BB-mode fluctuations for each method. We see that the improvement on foreground removal due to moment constraints is at the expense of increasing noise in the reconstructed CMB BB-mode map, as expected. Hence, there is a clear trade-off between mitigation of residual foreground contamination and noise degradation, but also a sweet spot where the noise penalty is more than compensated by the reduction of residual foreground contamination, depending on the observable of interest. As we will see in Sect. 4.2.4, for rr the optimal solution is given by cMILC06 for LiteBIRD.

Figure 5 summarizes the results for PICO in the BICEP2 region. As expected, the level of residual foregrounds and noise in the CMB BB-mode map reconstruction for PICO is further reduced compared to LiteBIRD due to higher sensitivity and broader spectral coverage (2020-800800 GHz). PICO also has the capability to probe second-order moments of the foreground emission. In particular, adding constraints on first- and second-order dust temperature moments, 𝒘T⋅∂Tdfdust=0\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial_{T_{d}}f_{\rm dust}=0 (cMILC08; fourth row) and 𝒘T⋅∂Td2fdust=0\boldsymbol{w}^{\rm T}\cdot\partial^{2}_{T_{d}}f_{\rm dust}=0 (cMILC09; bottom row), significantly reduces the residual foreground contamination at small scales. Again, the left column highlights the improvement in terms of residual foreground contamination when including more and more moments in cMILC, with best results obtained in the bottom row (cMILC09), where several moments of dust and synchrotron up to second order (fsync,fdust,∂βsfsync,∂βdfdust,∂Tdfdust,∂Td2fdust){(f_{\rm sync},f_{\rm dust},\partial_{\beta_{s}}f_{\rm sync},\partial_{\beta_{d}}f_{\rm dust},\partial_{T_{d}}f_{\rm dust},\partial^{2}_{T_{d}}f_{\rm dust})} were deprojected. As expected, additional moment constraints are at the expense of an increase of residual noise contamination (middle column), but remain at a reasonable level compared to the r.m.s of CMB BB-mode fluctuations (right column) thanks to the high sensitivity of PICO. The best trade-off for rr among those maps is actually given by cMILC08 for PICO, as we show in Sect. 4.2.4.

4.2.2 Statistical properties of residual foregrounds and noise

Besides map visualisation, it is instructive to look at the statistical properties of the residual foreground and noise contaminations in the recovered CMB BB-mode maps, which we present in Fig. 6 for LiteBIRD (upper panels) and PICO (lower panels).

In the left panels of Fig. 6, we computed the one-point statistics (probability distribution function – PDF) of the residual foreground contamination on fsky=50f_{\rm sky}=50% of the sky for the NILC CMB BB-mode map (red line) and for several cMILC CMB BB-mode maps, with more and more moments being deprojected. Similarly, in the right panels of Fig. 6, we show the PDF of the residual noise contamination for the same NILC and cMILC maps. Overall, the residual foreground and noise contamination is lower for PICO than LiteBIRD due to higher sensitivity and broader spectral coverage. As we already stressed in Sect. 3.4, the variance of the residual noise contamination (right panels) increases when adding constraints on moments in cMILC because of the increasing volume of the parameter space with respect to NILC. In stark contrast, the variance of the residual foreground contamination (left panels) significantly decreases by deprojecting moments with cMILC.

Clearly, the PDF of foreground residuals (left panels) shows larger variance and skewness for NILC (red line), while adding nulling constraints on zeroth- and first-order moments of dust and synchrotron (fsync,fdust,∂βsfsync,∂βdfdust,∂Tdfdust){(f_{\rm sync},f_{\rm dust},\partial_{\beta_{s}}f_{\rm sync},\partial_{\beta_{d}}f_{\rm dust},\partial_{T_{d}}f_{\rm dust})} with cMILC significantly reduces the variance and skewness of the residual foreground contamination (cMILC08; blue line), therefore leaving only negligible Gaussian residuals in the recovered CMB BB-mode map. More quantitatively, for LiteBIRD the variance of residual foregrounds is σFG2=0.05​σCMB2\sigma_{\rm FG}^{2}=0.05\thinspace\sigma_{\rm CMB}^{2} for NILC and σFG2=0.003​σCMB2\sigma_{\rm FG}^{2}=0.003\thinspace\sigma_{\rm CMB}^{2} for cMILC08, hence a reduction of the foreground variance by 9494% with cMILC. For PICO, the variance of residual foregrounds is σFG2=0.0025​σCMB2\sigma_{\rm FG}^{2}=0.0025\thinspace\sigma_{\rm CMB}^{2} for NILC and σFG2=0.0012​σCMB2\sigma_{\rm FG}^{2}=0.0012\thinspace\sigma_{\rm CMB}^{2} for cMILC10, hence a reduction of the foreground variance by 5252% with cMILC. Similarly, the skewness of residual foregrounds on fsky=50f_{\rm sky}=50% of the sky is ⟨sFG3⟩/σFG3=−0.3\langle s_{\rm FG}^{3}\rangle/\sigma_{\rm FG}^{3}=-0.3 for NILC and ⟨sFG3⟩/σFG3=0.18\langle s_{\rm FG}^{3}\rangle/\sigma_{\rm FG}^{3}=0.18 for cMILC08, hence a reduction of the residual skewness by 4040% with cMILC (with respect to the CMB r.m.s., the residual skewness is ⟨sFG3⟩/σCMB3=−3×10−3\langle s_{\rm FG}^{3}\rangle/\sigma_{\rm CMB}^{3}=-3\times 10^{-3} for NILC and ⟨sFG3⟩/σCMB3=4×10−5\langle s_{\rm FG}^{3}\rangle/\sigma_{\rm CMB}^{3}=4\times 10^{-5} for cMILC08). For PICO, the skewness of residual foregrounds is ⟨sFG3⟩/σFG3=−0.3\langle s_{\rm FG}^{3}\rangle/\sigma_{\rm FG}^{3}=-0.3 for NILC and ⟨sFG3⟩/σFG3=−0.11\langle s_{\rm FG}^{3}\rangle/\sigma_{\rm FG}^{3}=-0.11 for cMILC10, hence a reduction of the residual skewness by 6060% with cMILC (with respect to the CMB r.m.s., the residual skewness is ⟨sFG3⟩/σCMB3=−4×10−5\langle s_{\rm FG}^{3}\rangle/\sigma_{\rm CMB}^{3}=-4\times 10^{-5} for NILC and ⟨sFG3⟩/σCMB3=−5×10−6\langle s_{\rm FG}^{3}\rangle/\sigma_{\rm CMB}^{3}=-5\times 10^{-6} for cMILC10). Therefore, cMILC leads to a solution that minimizes foreground variance and skewness, largely beating NILC on that front. The trends observed in our numerical results are consistent with those predicted by the analytical expressions in Sect. 3.4.

4.2.3 BB-mode power spectrum

In Fig. 7 we compute the angular power spectrum of the residual foreground contamination (CℓfgdsC_{\ell}^{\rm fgds}; left panels) in the recovered CMB BB-mode maps on fsky=50%f_{\rm sky}=50\% of the sky, along with the standard deviation of the residual noise and lensing power spectra (2/(2​ℓ+1)​fsky​Cℓnoise/lensing{\sqrt{2/(2\ell+1)f_{\rm sky}}C_{\ell}^{\rm noise/lensing}}; right panels). The results from NILC and cMILC are shown for LiteBIRD in the upper panels and for PICO in the lower panels. The power spectra are deconvolved from the Galactic mask and the beam window function using MASTER (Hivon et al., 2002), and binned across multipoles with Δ​ℓ=16\Delta\ell=16. The same Galactic mask was used for the NILC and cMILC maps for fair comparison, but in principle the shape of the Galactic mask can be optimised for each variant of cMILC, since the morphology of the residual foreground contamination obviously differs, as is also suggested by the studies presented in Sec 4.2.1 and Sec. 4.2.2.

It is clear from the left panels of Fig. 7 that adding constraints on dust and synchrotron moments in cMILC significantly reduces the residual foreground contamination across a broad range of multipoles compared to NILC, and thus potentially prevents biases due to residual foregrounds in the recovered primordial CMB BB-mode power spectrum. In contrast, while the residual noise bias on the power spectrum can be corrected for using Jackknife, the noise error (standard deviation of residual noise power spectrum) increases when increasing the volume of the constrained parameter space in cMILC, as it is shown in the right panels of Fig. 7.

For LiteBIRD (upper left panel), while the power spectrum of residual foreground contamination for NILC (red line) is reduced well below the lensing BB-mode signal, it is still at a level equivalent to r≳3×10−3r\gtrsim 3\times 10^{-3} across the full range of multipoles. Therefore, after delensing, NILC would not guarantee proper recovery of the primordial CMB BB-mode power spectrum at r=10−3r=10^{-3}. In contrast, by adding constraints on more and more dust and synchrotron moments, cMILC helps reducing the level of residual foreground contamination in the recovered CMB BB-mode power spectrum down to r<10−3r<10^{-3} at recombination scales. In particular, deprojecting all zeroth- and first-order moments of the dust and synchrotron (cMILC08; blue line) enables significant reduction of the residual foreground contamination to CMB BB-modes for LiteBIRD, down to levels well below r=10−3r=10^{-3} at all multipoles.

Similarly, the lower left panel of Fig. 7 shows the power spectra of the residual foreground contamination for PICO after component separation with the NILC and cMILC methods. Due to its higher sensitivity and broader spectral coverage, PICO allows reducing foreground residuals well below the primordial CMB BB-mode power spectrum at r=10−3r=10^{-3} across the full range of multipoles covering both reionization and recombination scales, even with a blind NILC method. Still, cMILC enables further reduction of the residual foreground contamination to the CMB BB-mode power spectrum by deprojecting more and more foreground moments. We find that first- and second-order dust temperature moments (cMILC08, cMILC10, and cMILC12) lead to the lowest biases due to residual foreground contamination, reaching below the detection limit r=5×10−4r=5\times 10^{-4} of PICO (Hanany et al., 2019).

While deprojecting successively more moments with cMILC reduces the level of residual foreground contamination across a wide range of multipoles, for PICO the overall decrease of residuals actually breaks at the largest scales ℓ≲15\ell\lesssim 15, suggesting that our first-guess pivots, based on zeroth-order fits in the literature (Planck Collaboration X, 2016, e.g.), might not be appropriate for the largest angular scales, where averaging processes, and thus high-order moments, are the most significant. For sensitive experiments like PICO, high-order moments should thus be included in parametric SED fitting to revise zeroth-order pivots. In Sect. 5.1 and Fig. 10, we update the dust pivot temperature T¯d\overline{T}_{d} to show that, with revised pivots, cMILC is able to reduce the residual foreground contamination consistently at all mutipoles. However, a clear computational procedure for optimizing the pivots still requires more work, as we also explain in Sect. 5.1.

To conclude, cMILC provides quite spectacular results on foregrounds removal across all multipoles, thus significantly reducing biases on the CMB BB-mode power spectrum. However, there is a clear trade-off between residual foregrounds mitigation (left panels of Fig. 7) and noise degradation (right panels of Fig. 7) that needs to be appreciated to find the best combination of moments in cMILC that will lead to less biased but still sensitive constraints on the observable of interest, which here is rr (see Sect. 4.2.4).

4.2.4 Likelihood estimation of the tensor-to-scalar ratio

In this section, we perform the likelihood estimation of the recovered probability distribution of the tensor-to-scalar ratio rr after foreground removal with NILC and cMILC. We emphasize two important aspects: the irreducible bias on rr, or systematic error arising from residual foreground contamination (noting that noise and lensing biases on the power spectrum can usually be corrected for), and the statistical uncertainty σ⁡(r)\sigma(r). The latter has contributions from cosmic variance of the primordial signal, residual foregrounds, residual lensing signals and noise.

The power spectrum of the reconstructed CMB BB-mode map from either NILC or cMILC is

C^ℓBB=Cℓlens+C^ℓfgds+C^ℓnoise,\displaystyle\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm BB}_{\ell}=C^{\thinspace\rm lens}_{\ell}+\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm fgds}_{\ell}+\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm noise}_{\ell}, (59)

where CℓblensC^{\thinspace\rm lens}_{\ell_{b}} is the power spectrum of the CMB lensing BB-mode signal (r=0r=0, AL=1A_{L}=1), C^ℓfgds\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm fgds}_{\ell} the power spectrum of residual foregrounds (left panels of Fig. 7), and C^ℓnoise\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm noise}_{\ell} the noise power spectrum. The reconstructed CMB BB-mode map can be corrected for part of the cosmic variance of the lensing signal, either through internal delensing (Larsen et al., 2016; Carron et al., 2017; Millea et al., 2019) or through external lensing tracers (Sherwin & Schmittfull, 2015; Planck Collaboration et al., 2018a) such as cosmic infrared background maps (Planck Collaboration Int. XLVIII, 2016).

For our likelihood analysis, we will assume three levels of delensing: no delensing (AL=1A_{L}=1), 60%60\% delensing (AL=0.4A_{L}=0.4), and full delensing (AL=0A_{L}=0), such that after component separation and delensing the measured CMB BB-mode power spectrum is

C~ℓBB≡C^ℓBB−(1−AL)​Cℓlens=AL​Cℓlens+C^ℓfgds+C^ℓnoise.\displaystyle\tilde{C}^{\thinspace\rm BB}_{\ell}\equiv\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm BB}_{\ell}-(1-A_{L})\thinspace C^{\thinspace\rm lens}_{\ell}=A_{L}\thinspace C^{\thinspace\rm lens}_{\ell}+\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm fgds}_{\ell}+\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm noise}_{\ell}. (60)

The measured CMB BB-mode power spectrum, C~ℓBB\tilde{C}^{\thinspace\rm BB}_{\ell}, can in principle be corrected for the noise bias C^ℓnoise\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm noise}_{\ell} and for the residual lensing bias AL​CℓlensA_{L}\thinspace C^{\thinspace\rm lens}_{\ell}, so that after these corrections, any irreducible bias on the measured CMB BB-mode power spectrum arises from the residual foreground contamination:

C^ℓfgds=C~ℓBB−AL​Cℓlens−C^ℓnoise.\displaystyle\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm fgds}_{\ell}=\tilde{C}^{\thinspace\rm BB}_{\ell}-A_{L}\thinspace C^{\thinspace\rm lens}_{\ell}-\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm noise}_{\ell}. (61)

The binned likelihood (Hamimeche & Lewis, 2008) on the tensor-to-scalar ratio rr is thus built as

−2​ln⁡ℒ⁡(r)=∑ℓb,ℓb′(C^ℓbfgds−r​Cℓbprim)​Mℓb​ℓb′−1​(C^ℓb′fgds−r​Cℓb′prim),\displaystyle-2\ln\mathcal{L}\left(r\right)=\sum_{\ell_{b},\thinspace\ell^{\prime}_{b}}\left(\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm fgds}_{\ell_{b}}\thinspace-\thinspace r\thinspace C^{\thinspace\rm prim}_{\ell_{b}}\right){\rm M}^{-1}_{\ell_{b}\ell^{\prime}_{b}}\left(\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm fgds}_{\ell^{\prime}_{b}}\thinspace-\thinspace r\thinspace C^{\thinspace\rm prim}_{\ell^{\prime}_{b}}\right), (62)

where C^ℓfgds\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm fgds}_{\ell} is the power spectrum of residual foregrounds, CℓbprimC^{\thinspace\rm prim}_{\ell_{b}} is the primordial CMB BB-mode power spectrum model for a tensor-to-scalar ratio r=1r=1, and Mℓℓ′{\rm M}_{\ell\ell^{{}^{\prime}}} is the covariance matrix for a fiducial cosmological model with r=0r=0. Given that the input sky simulations do not contain any primordial signal, i.e. r=0r=0, the likelihood Eq. (62) thus computes the equivalent rr bias due to residual foreground contamination, and its significance with respect to the overall uncertainty due to cosmic variance of residual lensing, noise, and residual foregrounds, which are all included in the covariance matrix.

The binning, ℓb±Δ​ℓ/2\ell_{b}\pm\Delta\ell/2 with Δ​ℓ=16\Delta\ell=16, of the power spectra mitigates correlations between different ℓ\ell modes, so that off-diagonal terms of the covariance matrix can be neglected, thus leaving only the diagonal elements:

Mℓb​ℓb=2(2​ℓb+1)​fsky​Δ​ℓ​(C^ℓbBB−(1−AL)​Cℓblens)2,\displaystyle{\rm M}_{\ell_{b}\ell_{b}}={2\over\left(2\ell_{b}+1\right)f_{\rm sky}\Delta\ell}\left(\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm BB}_{\ell_{b}}-\left(1-A_{L}\right)C^{\thinspace\rm lens}_{\ell_{b}}\right)^{2}, (63)

which, according to Eq. (60), accounts for the cosmic variance of the residual lensing signal 2​(AL​Cℓlens)2/(2​ℓ+1){2(A_{L}C^{\thinspace\rm lens}_{\ell})^{2}/(2\ell+1)}, the sample variance of the residual foreground power spectrum 2​(C^ℓfgds)2/(2​ℓ+1){2(\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm fgds}_{\ell})^{2}/(2\ell+1)}, the sample variance of the noise power spectrum 2​(C^ℓnoise)2/(2​ℓ+1){2(\hat{C}^{\thinspace\rm noise}_{\ell})^{2}/(2\ell+1)}, and their cross-terms. The likelihood results on rr are obtained by summing modes between ℓmin=2{\ell_{\rm min}=2} and ℓmax=450{\ell_{\rm max}=450}, thus accounting for both the reionization and recombination bumps.

Figure 8 summarizes our results on the recovered tensor-to-scalar ratio rr after component separation with NILC or cMILC for both LiteBIRD and PICO, and for different levels of delensing. Biased detections (SNR≥2\geq 2) due to significant foreground residuals are shown in red with both 1​σ1\sigma (thick red) and 2​σ2\sigma (thin red) error bars, while for unbiased (SNR<2<2) measurements, the 95% upper bounds on rr are depicted by the thick green lines. As already observed on map reconstruction (Sect. 4.2.1-4.2.2) and power spectrum analysis (Sect. 4.2.3), adding constraints on an increasing number of moments with cMILC generally increases the uncertainty on rr due to noise degradation, but allows for eliminating biases on rr due to residual foreground contamination. This thus can help to robustly turn high significance but false detections with NILC into unbiased upper limits with the optimal choice of moment number in cMILC. However, the details depend on the experimental configuration and the overall level of delensing as we explain now.

The goal for full success of the LiteBIRD mission (Hazumi et al., 2019) is to achieve δ​r≲10−3\delta r\lesssim 10^{-3}, including both statistical and systematic uncertainties. For additional comparison, we thus define the simple metric

δ​r≡r2+σ2​(r=0),\displaystyle\delta r\equiv\sqrt{r^{2}+\sigma^{2}(r=0)}, (64)

which accounts for both the statistical error σ⁡(r=0)\sigma(r=0) and the systematic error, i.e. the residual bias rr with respect to r=0r=0. For LiteBIRD (upper panels of Fig. 8), NILC clearly leads to a significant bias on rr in our simulations, with r=(2.5±1.0)×10−3r=(2.5\pm 1.0)\times 10^{-3} in the absence of any delensing and r=(3.2±0.4)×10−3r=(3.2\pm 0.4)\times 10^{-3} in case of full delensing, which corresponds to a 3​σ3\sigma to 8​σ8\sigma bias on r=0r=0 and thus a cumulative systematic and statistical error of δ​r≳3×10−3\delta r\gtrsim 3\times 10^{-3}. Therefore, the systematic foreground residuals of NILC would not allow LiteBIRD to robustly reach its goals, even if the statistical uncertainties are sufficient. In contrast, for cMILC the bias on rr progressively decreases by deprojecting more and more foreground moments, with cMILC06, cMILC07, and cMILC08 all leading to unbiased measurements of r=0r=0, i.e. 2​σ2\sigma upper limits. Among these three unbiased versions, we see that for LiteBIRD cMILC06 (fsync,fdust,∂βfdust{f_{\rm sync},f_{\rm dust},\partial_{\beta}\thinspace f_{\rm dust}}) provides the best trade-off between bias mitigation and noise degradation on rr, with r=(0.7±1.1)×10−3r=(0.7\pm 1.1)\times 10^{-3} consistent with unbiased measurement of r=0r=0, while accumulating a systematic and statistical errors as low as δ​r≃σ⁡(r=0)≃10−3{\delta r\simeq\sigma(r=0)\simeq 10^{-3}}. This would allow a constraint on rr that is in line with the goals for LiteBIRD. Deprojecting dust temperature moments ∂Tfdust\partial_{T}f_{\rm dust} (cMILC08) would further reduce residual foreground biases down to r≲0.3×10−3r\lesssim 0.3\times 10^{-3}, but the limited spectral coverage of LiteBIRD at high frequency does not seem to provide enough sensitivity to constrain dust temperature moments and the noise degradation for cMILC08 starts blowing up. Finally, increasing the level of delensing helps reducing statistical uncertainties on rr for NILC and low-order cMILC. In contrast, the gain is less significant for the most-constrained versions of cMILC like cMILC06, because noise dominates over the lensing error for LiteBIRD (see upper right panel of Fig. 7).

For PICO (lower panels of Fig. 8), we can generally say that the overall degradation of the statistical error is not as large when including progressively more moments until about cMILC10. This is due to the broad frequency coverage and high channel sensitivity of PICO, which allows us to extract a lot of extra information even beyond rr. However, the overall performance of the method for recovery of rr depends significantly on the level of delensing. Assuming full delensing (left panel), NILC would yield r=(2.2±0.4)×10−4r=(2.2\pm 0.4)\times 10^{-4}, which corresponds to a 5​σ5\sigma bias on r=0r=0 due to residual foreground contamination, while cMILC allows to reduce the bias on rr by progressively deprojecting more moments of the foregrounds. For now omitting the optimised hybrid case cMILC12 (which we will return to in Sect. 5.2), for PICO, cMILC08 (fsync,fdust,∂βfsync,∂βfdust,∂Tfdust{f_{\rm sync},f_{\rm dust},\partial_{\beta}\thinspace f_{\rm sync},\partial_{\beta}\thinspace f_{\rm dust},\partial_{T}\thinspace f_{\rm dust}}) provides the best results, giving r=(0.7±0.9)×10−4r=(0.7\pm 0.9)\times 10^{-4} consistent with r=0r=0, and hence a cumulative systematic and statistical error as low as δ​r≃10−4\delta r\simeq 10^{-4}. Due to high-frequency coverage above 500500 GHz, PICO allows to constrain dust temperature moments ∂Tfdust\partial_{T}f_{\rm dust} (cMILC08) with enough sensitivity to control residual foreground biases, while still mitigating the noise degradation. Nevertheless, for Alens=0A_{\rm lens}=0, we can see that all considered methods, including NILC, provide tight constraints on rr, with biases typically smaller than r=5×10−4r=5\times 10^{-4}, which is the target detection of PICO (Hanany et al., 2019). For partial delensing, all the considered methods provide quite consistent results on rr, compatible with r=0r=0, since the residual lensing error dominates over the noise for PICO (see lower right panel of Fig. 7). However, as we will show below, pivot optimization can affect this behaviour.

Overall our results indicate, NILC alone does not lead to unbiased estimates of rr in the case of LiteBIRD, but has a good performance for PICO. By applying cMILC, these limitations can be overcome and even PICO’s constraints on rr could be further improved. It also seems that with the d1s1 simulations inclusion of first order moments suffices for constraints on rr, even if PICO does show sensitivity to the second order moment of TdT_{d}.

4.2.5 More complex foreground models: MHD simulation with line-of-sight contributions

As stressed by Tassis & Pavlidou (2015), the effective SED of the Galactic thermal dust foreground emission must be less trivial than a simple modified blackbody because of the average of multiple cloud contributions of various emissivities, temperatures, and magnetic fields orientations along the line-of-sight, thus leading to some decorrelation of the polarized dust emission across frequencies. The moments of the effective foreground emission resulting from line-of-sight averaging effects can in principle be deprojected with cMILC. In this section, we thus investigate the performance of cMILC on sky simulations having non-trivial foreground complexity, by using publicly available MHD-model simulations77 7 https://zzz.physics.umn.edu/ipsig/20180424_dc_maps (model 96). that were produced for the PICO data challenge.

In this sky simulation, the dust and synchrotron emissions are consistently derived from MHD simulations of the magnetic field turbulence in the interstellar medium (Kritsuk et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019), with the dust model described in Hensley (2015). The MHD-model simulation is particularly interesting because of integrating multiple modified blackbodies of varying temperatures and spectral indices along the line-of-sight, so that the resulting dust SED in each pixel will not be a perfect modified blackbody, which makes this foreground model both more realistic and more challenging for parametric fitting methods aiming at BB-mode component separation. The CMB and noise realisations in the MHD simulation are the same as those in the d1s1 simulation.

Figure 9 summarises the cMILC results on the residual foregrounds and noise contamination to the CMB BB-mode power spectrum for the MHD simulation (upper panels), together with the results on the recovered tensor-to-scalar ratio (lower panels). By deprojecting foregrounds moments with the semi-blind method cMILC, we are able to tackle the foreground complexity arising from line-of-sight effects in the MHD simulation, and again reduce the residual foreground foreground contamination further than NILC. The best results on rr for the MHD simulation are obtained with cMILC03 and cMILC06. For 60%60\% delensing, cMILC06 provides r=(0.3±0.8)×10−4r=\left(0.3\pm 0.8\right)\times 10^{-4} consistent with r=0r=0, and a cumulation of systematic and statistical errors of δ​r=r2+σ2​(r)≲2.1×10−4{\delta r=\sqrt{r^{2}+\sigma^{2}(r)}\lesssim 2.1\times 10^{-4}}, which reduces down to δ​r≲8.5×10−5{\delta r\lesssim 8.5\times 10^{-5}} in the case of full delensing.

Interestingly, deprojecting the first- and second-order moments of synchrotron in cMILC08, cMILC09, cMILC10, and cMILC11 tends to degrade the results for the MHD simulation. We interpret this behaviour as being caused by the way the MHD simulation has been built: while the dust emission has spectral variations along the line-of-sight and across the sky, the synchrotron index is uniform in the MHD simulation (Brandon S. Hensley, private communication). This implies that higher-order moments of the synchrotron spectral index do not contribute in this simulation, and any constraints that nulls synchrotron components in cMILC will only increase the variance of the unconstrained foregrounds and noise. This also highlights that cMILC can provide a solid diagnosis of the level of spectral complexity of each foreground.

Overall our analysis shows that cMILC is a quite robust component separation method, which without any extra modifications also allows to handle foregrounds complexity arising from line-of-sight and other averaging effects. In addition, the effect of unmodeled spectral complexity is successfully reduced by means of the blind variance minimization within cMILC.

5 Discussion

While the previous sections demonstrated some general aspects of cMILC, reaching the full potential of the method and comparison to other methods requires more work. Here, we first discuss some possible optimisations of cMILC (Sects. 5.1 and 5.2), and then briefly mention the relevance to ground-based CMB experiments (Sect. 5.3), and other observables and figures of merit (Sect. 5.4).

5.1 On the importance of optimal pivot parameters

Throughout our analysis, we have been using first-guess pivots {β¯s,β¯d,T¯d}{\{\overline{\beta}_{s},\overline{\beta}_{d},\overline{T}_{d}\}} in cMILC (Eq. 42), based on the mean spectral index and temperature of dust and synchrotron issued from the current knowledge on intensity foregrounds (Planck Collaboration X, 2016, e.g.). In the language of moment expansion, these first-guess pivots from the literature typically result from fitting a zeroth-order model to the effective SED of the foreground emission:

I⁡(ν)\displaystyle I(\nu) =A1​fsync​(ν,βs)+A2​fdust​(ν,βd,Td),\displaystyle=A_{1}\thinspace f_{\rm sync}(\nu,\beta_{s})+A_{2}\thinspace f_{\rm dust}(\nu,\beta_{d},T_{d})\thinspace, (65)

where the pivots, i.e. βs,βd​ and ​Td\beta_{s},\beta_{d}\textrm{ and }T_{d}, are fit in each pixel and then averaged. As such, the zeroth-order model Eq. (65) might not provide the best fit at the largest angular scales, where averaging effects and higher-order moment corrections become relevant to the SED. As pointed out above, in Fig. 7 for PICO d1s1 one can see that the performance of cMILC in reducing foreground contamination is spectacular on a large range of multipoles but non-optimal at the lowest multipoles ℓ≲15\ell\lesssim 15, which are most relevant for constraining rr. This suggests that first-guess pivots derived from traditional zeroth-order moment fits (Eq. 65) might not be optimal for cleaning foregrounds at the largest angular scales, where averaging effects, and thus higher-order moments, become relevant. Another complication is that the optimal pivots will generally depend on the type of method that is employed, given that analysis choices vary but directly introduce averaging effects.

To investigate this point further, we thus modified the pivot values in the first needlet band to evaluate the impact on the performance of cMILC at low ℓ\ell. In particular, we found that lowering the pivot value for the dust temperature down to T¯d=16\overline{T}_{d}=16  K actually improves the performance of cMILC in cleaning foregrounds at low ℓ\ell, and shows a more consistent picture of monotonic reduction of the bias on rr when deprojecting more and more moments with cMILC. The results for PICO d1s1 simulation with the updated pivot temperature are shown in Fig. 10. A progressive reduction of the bias on rr, without much noise penalty, is clear from cMILC01 to cMILC08, while it actually breaks for higher-order constraints (cMILC09, cMILC10, cMILC11), suggesting that a proper optimisation of all the pivots would probably be required instead of this simple ad-hoc variation of the pivot temperature. Still, these results highlight how the performance of cMILC is sensitive to the choice of pivots at low ℓ\ell, and the importance of choosing the most appropriate pivot parameters for the moment expansion. While a full optimisation of the pivots using sophisticated parametric pivot fitting algorithms deserves an in-depth work that is beyond the scope of this paper, hereafter we highlight a few important aspects.

We attempted optimizing the pivots by extracting mean polarisation SEDs from our simulation. However, for polarisation the definition of an average SED is not as straightforward, given that no polarisation ’monopole’ exists. This makes it hard to define a concrete metric for the pivot optimization. This metric is also expected to directly depend on other analysis choices such as real-space versus harmonic-space analysis.

Besides, further optimisation of cMILC would probably be possible by using local pivots across different regions of the sky. While here we have been using uniform pivot parameters across the sky throughout our analysis, the all-sky average temperature and spectral index of the dust and synchrotron differ from the local mean index and temperature in a certain region of the sky, e.g., in the BICEP2 region. Therefore, a possible improvement of the cMILC method would be to adopt different pivot parameters in different sky regions and perform a local moment expansion. One open question is then how to optimally combine the results from the various regions to constraint on rr.

Finally, further optimisation of cMILC could potentially be achieved for the localisation of filtering in both pixel space and harmonic space, through the investigation of different needlet windows in terms of number, shape, and width in order to determine whether the performance of the foreground cleaning would benefit from more localisation of the filter in pixel space or more localisation in harmonic space. All this outlines a high-dimensional optimisation problem that will be carried out in the future.

5.2 Hybrid moments across multipole ranges

The relative contribution of the different moments of dust and synchrotron, e.g., Aνs​(βs−β¯s)​∂βsfsync{A_{\nu_{s}}(\beta_{s}-\overline{\beta}_{s})\partial_{\beta_{s}}f_{\rm sync}} versus Aνd​(βd−β¯d)​∂βdfdust{A_{\nu_{d}}(\beta_{d}-\overline{\beta}_{d})\partial_{\beta_{d}}f_{\rm dust}}, to the overall foreground power spectrum is likely to vary across multipoles. In particular, we experienced that the first-order synchrotron index moment had more constraining power at low multipoles ℓ≤50\ell\leq 50, while the first-order dust index moment was helping more at ℓ>50\ell>50. Given that cMILC is performed on a needlet frame (see Fig. 3), it allows us to set different combinations of moment constraints for different multipole windows in order to optimise the trade-off between residual foreground biases and noise degradation across multipoles.

To explore this idea further, we thus implemented a hybrid version cMILC12 (see Table 1), which deprojects the moments fsync,fdust,∂βfsync,∂Tfdust{f_{\rm sync},f_{\rm dust},\partial_{\beta}\thinspace f_{\rm sync},\partial_{T}\thinspace f_{\rm dust}} in the first two needlet bands and the moments fsync,fdust,∂βfdust,∂Tfdust{f_{\rm sync},f_{\rm dust},\partial_{\beta}\thinspace f_{\rm dust},\partial_{T}\thinspace f_{\rm dust}} at higher multipoles ℓ>50\ell>50. As shown in Fig. 8 and Fig. 10, the hybrid version cMILC12 provides the best trade-off and result of the analysis, with both the lowest bias on rr due to residual foregrounds and the smallest statistical uncertainty due to low noise degradation: r=(0.4±0.5)×10−4r=(0.4\pm 0.5)\times 10^{-4} consistent with an unbiased recovery of r=0r=0, and a cumulative systematic and statistical errors of δ​r=r2+σ​(r)2<6×10−5{\delta r=\sqrt{r^{2}+\sigma(r)^{2}}<6\times 10^{-5}}. cMILC is thus quite flexible by allowing for different combinations of moments across multipoles.

With future foreground observations, it will be possible to use cMILC for diagnostics of the most relevant moments of the foreground emission for each ranges of multipoles. Furthermore, given that the various moments of the non-Gaussian foreground contamination are spatially correlated with each other, it would in principle be possible to compress the number of moments into a small set of independent components ranked by their relevance to optimise foreground cleaning with cMILC. These ideas also have to be worked out more cleanly in the future.

5.3 Ground-based surveys

For future ground-based CMB surveys, like SO (Ade et al., 2019) and CMB-S4 (Abazajian et al., 2016), it is more difficult to directly probe the reionization peak of the primordial CMB BB-mode at the lowest multipoles ℓ≲15\ell\lesssim 15 because only a fraction of the sky from the ground is accessible. Hence, future ground-based CMB experiments will have to rely mainly on information from the recombination peak (i.e. 30≤ℓ≤20030\leq\ell\leq 200) to constrain rr. In addition, the number of available frequency bands for ground-based experiments is limited by atmospheric windows, which will limit the number of foreground moments that can be deprojected by cMILC.

However, as evident from the left panels of Fig. 7, the deprojection of only two or three foreground moments with cMILC is already very successful around the recombination peak, with the reduction of the residual foreground contamination of cMILC in comparison to NILC being most significant at intermediate multipoles 30≤ℓ≤20030\leq\ell\leq 200. Therefore, cMILC would be particularly helpful also for future ground-based CMB surveys in removing residual foreground biases on rr. With upcoming ground-based experiments like CCAT-prime (Aravena et al., 2019), which will provide wider frequency coverage owing to improved atmospheric transparency, we may anticipate significant benefits of using cMILC. However, dedicated forecasts are required taking differences in the frequency coverage and angular resolution into account.

5.4 Other observables and figures of merit

While in this work we focused on component separation for BB-modes, with rr defining the figure of merit, cMILC is also directly applicable to CMB temperature and EE-mode analyses relevant to other observables. As shown in Fig. 7, the potential of cMILC in removing foregrounds through moments significantly improves towards small angular scales. The details may change with further optimizations of cMILC, but generally we expect that cMILC could also help improve constraints on cosmological parameters such as NeffN_{\rm eff} and ∑mν\sum m_{\nu}, which depend on damping tail physics (Abazajian et al., 2015, e.g.,). Additional benefits may become apparent for studies of the Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) power spectrum (Komatsu & Seljak, 2002; Hill & Pajer, 2013; Bolliet et al., 2019, e.g.,), which again rely on information gleaned from small scale fluctuations.

Our method could also provide gains in future searches for primordial non-Gaussinity and CMB lensing/delensing analyses. As shown for the one-point statistics of foreground residuals in Fig. 6, cMILC allows significantly reducing non-Gaussian foreground contamination in the CMB map by deprojecting moments. Since CMB lensing (Hu & Okamoto, 2002, e.g.) and bispectrum estimators (Bucher et al., 2010, e.g.) rely on the extraction of non-Gaussian features (no matter if primordial or generated by lensing), they are prone to non-Gaussian foreground residuals in the CMB map (Hill, 2018; van Engelen et al., 2014, e.g.), and thus to be potentially biased depending on the sensitivity of future experiments. This aspect deserves further investigation but is beyond the present scope.

6 Conclusions

For robust measurements of the tensor-to-scalar ratio rr as a signature of primordial gravitational waves from inflation, it is essential to minimise both statistical and systematic errors due to residual foregrounds in component separation analyses. Statistical uncertainties σ⁡(r)\sigma(r) arise from the cosmic/sample variance of the residual lensing, foreground, and noise contaminations after component separation and delensing, while systematic errors, leading to biases on rr, arise from the residual foreground contamination to the CMB BB-mode power spectrum after component separation. Hence, reliable foreground cleaning is achieved by minimizing cumulative systematic and statistical errors δ​r=(r−rtrue)2+σ2​(r){\delta r=\sqrt{\left(r-r^{\thinspace\rm true}\right)^{2}+\sigma^{2}(r)}}.

In the present work, we developed the new semi-blind component separation method cMILC, which deprojects the main statistical moments of the foregrounds without altering the CMB BB-mode signal, thus allowing to reduce systematic errors (or biases) on rr due to residual foreground contamination, while still mitigating statistical uncertainties (see Figs. 8, 9, 10). By applying cMILC to sky simulations with varying foreground complexity for experimental settings similar to those of LiteBIRD and PICO, we have identified specific combinations of foreground moments that optimise the trade-off between residual foreground biases and noise degradation for constraints on rr. In particular, the cMILC method allows us to reach the sensitivity goals on rr of both LiteBIRD and PICO mission concepts, by removing biases on rr without excessive noise penalties, thus overcoming limitations of NILC.

We show that for LiteBIRD a deprojection of the first-order moment of the dust spectral index (Table 1: cMILC06) is needed for unbiased detection of r=0r=0 (see Fig. 8). In this case, the cumulative systematic and statistical errors (i.e. bias + variance) is δ​r=r2+σ2​(r)≲10−3{\delta r=\sqrt{r^{2}+\sigma^{2}(r)}\lesssim 10^{-3}}, where the blind NILC method would exceed δ​r≳3×10−3\delta r\gtrsim 3\times 10^{-3} due to more than 3​σ3\sigma residual foreground bias on r=0r=0. For PICO, deprojecting the first-order moments of the dust spectral index and dust temperature (Table 1: cMILC08) provides the best unbiased results on rr without much noise penalty (see Figs. 8, 10). This yields r=(0.7±0.9)×10−4r=\left(0.7\pm 0.9\right)\times 10^{-4}, and hence a cumulative systematic and statistical error as low as δ​r≃10−4{\delta r\simeq 10^{-4}}.

While our analysis shows that for constraints on rr in principle only first moments are needed, PICO is further sensitive to the second moment of the dust temperature. This conclusion is expected to be a strong function of the complexity of the foreground simulation, and thus may not hold for more complicated skies. In the presence of multiple dust modified blackbodies along the line-of-sight (Fig. 9 in Sect. 4.2.5), cMILC still performs well and helps reducing residual foreground contaminations and the bias on rr without paying much noise penalty. Our analysis further shows that the optimization of pivots plays an important role (Sect. 5.1), requiring more investigation. These findings highlight the potential of cMILC as a robust foreground cleaning method but also diagnostic tool, enabling to test the sky complexity in future analysis.

The ability of cMILC to peel off foregrounds through the deprojection of their spectral moments is not limited to the search for primordial BB-modes and constraints on rr, but could as well be exploited for CMB temperature and EE-mode analyses to improve constraints on other cosmological parameters like ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} and NeffN_{\rm eff}. By getting rid of non-Gaussian residuals (Fig. 6 and Sect. 4.2.2), cMILC is also of great interest to searches for primordial non-Gaussianity and in the CMB lensing reconstruction. cMILC would also be helpful for the extraction of other faint cosmological signals such as SZ effects and anisotropic primordial spectral distortions. Forecasts for ground-based experiments should consider these additional observables in the analysis.

We also stress that moments of the foreground emission result not only from integrating multiple contributions along the line-of-sight, but also arise from several averaging processes across the sky like beam convolutions, spherical harmonic transforms, Q,UQ,U to E,BE,B transforms, and other filtering processes (e.g. needlets). In fact, future CMB surveys will deliver sky maps of varying native beam resolutions at different frequencies. At low frequencies, the beams are typically larger than at high frequencies, and hence averaging processes are intrinsically larger at the map level. If not properly taken into account when combining maps, this will lead to inevitable decorrelation across frequencies. In addition, while most of the averaging effects can be propagated analytically, line-of-sight averaging is unavoidable, thus requiring a more general SED treatment even at the pixel level. All the above aspects pose a challenge for foreground modelling and the search for primordial BB-modes that cannot be ignored. Robustly deprojecting the moments of dust and synchrotron emissions that arise from averaging/decorrelation effects is thus crucial to avoid systematic errors from residual foreground contamination that will bias the faint primordial BB-mode signal, hence the tensor-to-scalar ratio. The cMILC method provides an avenue forward this direction.

While here we specifically focused on a comparison to NILC, not only will it be important to extend this comparison to other methods but one should also think about augmenting other methods using moments. For instance, we anticipate that moment expansion approaches can help parametric component separation methods in the search for primordial BB-modes, providing a systematic way of extending the list of expected foreground parameters. The optimal method will also strongly depend on the observable under consideration, which further motivates more extensive comparisons of various cleaning methods in the future, ultimately preparing us for the analysis challenges in the years to come.

Appendix A Flexibility of cMILC concerning pivot parameter values

By construction, cMILC allows for some flexibility in the assumed pivot values of the foreground parameters. For a set of assumed pivot values, the nulling constraints of cMILC (Eq. 42) enable to null any part of the foreground emission that projects onto the moments centred on these pivots, without altering the CMB signal due to the conservation constraint. Should there be any small departures in the data from the assumed pivot values then a part of the foreground contamination cannot be fully deprojected, but such unconstrained foreground contamination is anyway handled by blind variance minimization, like NILC would proceed. To illustrate the margin on the choice of pivot values, in Fig. 11 we show the performance of cMILC in terms of residual foreground contamination for different pivot values, as compared to NILC.
